proposedchanges.title: Trump Disbands Election Integrity Commission After Voter-Data Dispute
proposedchanges.description_long: The Presidential Advisory Commission on Election Integrity was created to investigate claims of voter fraud. Vice President Mike Pence chaired it, and Kansas Secretary of State Kris Kobach served as vice chair. The commission's requests for detailed voter information drew objections from states and privacy advocates, who questioned federal collection and intended use of the data. President Donald Trump announced the commission's termination on January 3, 2018, after states resisted the requests and the panel faced legal and public scrutiny. The commission closed before issuing a final report, so it produced no findings establishing widespread voter fraud. Its proposed inquiry ended without a formal public conclusion from the panel. The episode centered on the federal request for voter information and the state resistance it prompted. The closure left no commission findings on the fraud claims that had prompted its creation.
organization_tags: Presidential Advisory Commission on Election Integrity

evidencebasis: The original packet and latest descriptions identify the commission, its disputed voter-data requests, state resistance, and termination on January 3, 2018. The latest long names Pence and Kobach and confirms that the commission issued no final report.
notes: The proposed long removes source-audit language and preserves the distinction between the claims that motivated the panel and findings it never issued. The New York Times URL is retained.

proposedchanges.title: Trump Signs Section 230 Order After Twitter Labels Mail-Voting Posts
proposedchanges.description_short: Trump's 2020 order sought agency action on Section 230 after Twitter labeled his mail-voting posts.
proposedchanges.description_long: On May 28, 2020, President Donald Trump signed the executive order “Preventing Online Censorship” after Twitter added fact-check labels to his posts about mail-in voting. The order targeted social-media moderation and Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act. Section 230 protects platforms from some liability for user-posted content and permits good-faith content moderation. The order directed federal agencies to examine whether moderation decisions the administration considered biased should affect those protections. Trump argued that platforms were censoring his speech. The action followed a public dispute between the president and Twitter over the platform's treatment of his election claims. An executive order could direct agencies to review the law but could not repeal or rewrite Section 230 by itself. It therefore set a federal policy position and sought agency action; it did not itself remove platforms' existing legal protections. The order framed the moderation dispute as a federal policy issue while the statute remained in force.

evidencebasis: The latest medium describes an order aimed at moderation and Section 230 that directed agencies to pursue changes, and distinguishes that effort from congressional repeal. The supplied packet identifies Twitter's fact-check labels and the executive order.
notes: The proposed long retains the reported sequence and legal distinction without presenting motive or later platform conduct as proven. All four source URLs from the merged record remain intact.
